walkthroughs.body_html:
Introduction to Economics — a core area of Economics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Introduction to Economics brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Introduction to Economics.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Ricardo published 'Principles of Political Economy and Taxation' in:

options: Structural unemployment is unemployment caused by a recession.
Structural unemployment is when people are too lazy to work.
Unemployment caused by a mismatch between workers' skills/location and available jobs — often due to long-term economic change like deindustrialisation.
The fiscal multiplier is the rate of growth of the money supply.

mcqs.q: What determines the size of the fiscal multiplier?
options: The fiscal multiplier is the rate of growth of the money supply.
Aggregate demand is the same as GDP measured by demand.
Mainly the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) — the higher the share of extra income people spend domestically, the bigger the multiplier. Leakages (saving, imports, taxes) reduce the multiplier.
The fiscal multiplier is always 2 or 3.

mcqs.q: What components make up aggregate demand?
options: AD = C + I + G + (X - M): consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports. A shift in any component shifts the AD curve.
Aggregate demand is the same as GDP measured by demand.
Aggregate demand is just the total amount consumers want to buy.
The fiscal multiplier is the rate of growth of the money supply.
